decision.title: Faster regex matching: ASCII member sets, a start filter, idle matchers, character repetitions (packet )
decision.summary: Regex matching gains an per class, a that skips impossible start positions, an kept in the cache entry, and instructions.

item.p: Whom it serves: every caller of the regex functions and of XSD pattern facets on short ASCII text, where after matching was the cost: 200,000 matches("abc_def ghi " || ., "\w+\s\w+\s\d+") took 0.38 s here against 0.13 s with contains (the packet measured 0.80 and 0.12 s on another machine).

Profile (callgrind, release, 20,000 such calls): 18,300 instructions a call, 13,300 in fn:matches; 10,700 matching (18 binary searches of the category runs by sxml_regex_is_word_character, 16 slot saves and pushes of the five-instruction loops of \w+, an attempt at every start position), 1,850 in compile_pattern, 1,050 of them making the matcher.
Mechanisms (glossary , , , ), all in the one engine:

ASCII fast paths: tools/generate-regex-tables.py emits the general categories of codepoints 0 to 127 as a table read before the runs (so collation, format and full-text lookups gain too) and sxml_regex_find_ascii_category_members; each class gets its ASCII member set when compiled (the union of its items, negation, case variants, less its subtraction, decided as sxml_regex_class_item_contains decides), so an ASCII class test is one bit test; an ASCII byte is read without the codepoint iterator. Non-ASCII characters take the items as before.

Start filter: a walk over the instructions before the first read (saves, jumps, splits, progress checks, counted loop bookkeeping; a fixed stack of 32 and at most 256 visits, ) collects the first characters a match can read and whether a path starts with "^"; any assertion, back-reference or empty match reached first leaves it unused. A search skips the positions it excludes without an attempt, but each still counts one step, as the failing first instruction of an attempt did, so the step limit and charged steps stay as before for them (the step bound test of tests/xpath_test.c needs that).

Idle matcher: a regex cache entry keeps the matcher of the last call that used it, reset by the new internal sxml_regex_matcher_reset (grown backtrack stack released, last search forgotten), counted in the cache's 8 MiB bound; a call that finds it in use (a replacement function using the same regex) makes its own, and a matcher made while the heap's limit is reached first evicts the unused entries, as 's compile does. The step limit stays per call.

Character repetition: a greedy x*, x+ or x{n,} whose atom is one instruction reading one character (a literal, a class, a case-blind literal, ".") compiles to REPEAT_CHARACTER followed by that instruction, not the loop of split, save, x, progress check and jump. It reads every character x matches, one step each (the failing one too, within the step limit), and pushes two entries, a floor and one that gives the characters back a codepoint at a time (F&O 4.0, section 6.1.4: longest first). Positive assertions drop both, negative ones undo them, like other choices. The counting pass knows the atom from the last instruction emitted, so both passes emit alike. Steps are the instructions run: a repetition counts one per character where the loop counted five, so a long greedy run charges fewer steps than before.
Measured, cumulatively (valgrind instructions of the whole process, 10^6; release, x86_64): before / +1 / +2 / +3 / +4
20,000 matches \w+\s\w+\s\d+: 366.9 / 285.8 / 284.4 / 259.4 / 200.3 (fn:matches 13,300 to about 4,800 instructions a call);

5,000 distinct regexes compiled ("x" || . || "[a-z]\w\d"): 180.7 / 196.9 / 194.2 / 199.7 / 199.7, about 3,800 instructions more a compile (the member sets; a first version that asked every class of every ASCII codepoint cost 32,000). Processor seconds, fastest of seven: regex-match.xq 1.069 / 0.866 / 0.791 / 0.822 / 0.652; regex-reuse.xq 0.250 / 0.203 / 0.169 / 0.155 / 0.146; 200,000 matches \w+\s\w+\s\d+ 0.382 / 0.269 / 0.259 / 0.234 / 0.197 (contains: 0.127), so a match costs about 0.35 instead of 1.3 microseconds over the loop; with [a-z_]+ [a-z]+ [0-9]+ 0.241 to 0.171. Not done: a search for a literal prefix; the start filter already skips every position whose first character cannot begin a match, and no benchmark here had a long literal prefix, so it was not measured.

Checked: QT4 XP40 and XQ40 fn-analyze-string, fn-matches, fn-matches.re, fn-matching-segments, fn-regex, fn-replace, fn-tokenize and XT40 analyze-string, regex, regex-syntax, regex-syntax-xslt20 with the release drivers: 4,405 pass, 10 fail, 1 wrong error, 1,154 not run, before and after, 0 outcomes differ case by case. 14,400 random regexes (classes, case-blind, assertions, quantifiers, groups) over random inputs of up to 40 characters give the same fn:analyze-string output as before.

Left: reluctant repetitions (x*?) still run as loops; a repetition of a group is a loop. A large query whose regex search ends in LIMIT_EXCEEDED reports the description of an earlier error that a try/catch caught (the error record is not cleared): seen with the random regexes, the same before and after, outside this packet.

Benchmarks: tests/bench/regex-reuse.xq () and tests/bench/regex-match.xq are not yet in tests/bench/run-bench.py (perf-5 held it); whoever next changes it registers both as ("regex-reuse", ["SXML", "xquery", os.path.join(BENCH, "regex-reuse.xq")]) and likewise for regex-match.
